section.title: Warning examples
section.p: Improper integrals are limits. That one sentence prevents many errors.

The errors below are common because they look like ordinary applications of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. But the Fundamental Theorem applies directly only on intervals where the integrand is continuous. When the interval is infinite or the integrand blows up, the limit must be handled first.

exercise.title: Why can a formal antiderivative still give a nonsense definite integral?

statement.p: Subtracting -1/x from -1 to 1 for \int_{-1}^{1}(1/x^2)\,dx produces a negative number for a positive integrand. In your own words, why is the Fundamental Theorem not a license to jump across a singularity, and what must you do instead?

hint.p: Part II requires continuity on the interval. Split at the blow-up and replace each dangerous endpoint by a limit. If either side diverges, the whole integral diverges.

subsection.title: Cancellation hides divergence
subsection.p: Some divergent improper integrals look harmless because positive and negative parts cancel symmetrically.

So one might think the integral is 0.
But that is not the definition of the improper integral. Because the singularity is at 0, we must split:
Neither piece converges to a finite number. Therefore
The symmetric cancellation gives a different object called a principal value:
That principal value exists, but it is not the improper integral.

figure.caption: The positive and negative pieces of 1/x cancel symmetrically, but each piece has infinite size.

note.title: Moral
note.p: For an improper integral over a singular point, each side must converge separately. Cancellation of two infinite pieces is not convergence.

exercise.title: Why is cancellation of two infinite pieces not convergence?

statement.p: Some improper integrals look harmless because positive and negative parts cancel symmetrically. In your own words, why must each side of a singularity converge separately, and why is an infinite plus-and-minus cancellation not a finite accumulated amount?

hint.p: Convergence is a statement about limits of proper integrals. Two divergences with opposite signs do not produce a well-defined limit of the sum.

subsection.p: A computer algebra system may return an antiderivative that is correct only on part of the real line, or correct only after choosing a complex logarithm branch.

note.title: Moral
note.p: A symbolic antiderivative must be checked on the interval where it is used. For real calculus, logarithms often need absolute values or a different expression on a different interval.

exercise.title: Why must a symbolic antiderivative be checked on the interval where it is used?

statement.p: A computer may return \frac12\ln(x^2-1) for \int x/(x^2-1)\,dx, which is not even defined on (-1,1) as a real logarithm. In your own words, why can a formally correct derivative still be the wrong real formula on the interval you care about?

hint.p: Real logarithms often need absolute values, and different intervals can require different expressions. Differentiate, then ask where the returned formula actually lives.

subsection.p: Improper integrals have given us one last lesson for exact integration: before computing, ask where the integral is defined and what limit is being taken.
This chapter has focused on exact methods and convergence. But exact antiderivatives are not always available, and convergence alone may not give the number we need. The next question is practical:
subsection.md: \text{How can we approximate an accumulated amount, and how can we control the error?}
subsection.p: That question leads to numerical integration.

exercise.title: Why can a trigonometric-substitution triangle fail on another interval?

statement.p: A formula derived from x=2\sec\theta with 0\le\theta<\pi/2 is built for x\ge2. In your own words, why can blindly reusing that formula for x<-2 change the answer, and what does that say about indefinite integrals on disconnected domains?

hint.p: A triangle carries sign information. Separate pieces of the domain, such as (-\infty,-2) and (2,\infty), may need different ranges or different inverse functions.
